name: Ọ́lọ̀mà
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 2 other works consulted do not discuss stress.
catalog_citation: Ajani, Japhet Onaolapo. 2023. The phonology of Ọ́lọ̀mà. PhD dissertation, Interdisciplinary Program in Linguistics, Tulane University, New Orleans. 342 pp. Open access via Tulane University Libraries (Alma-D MMS 9945513377406326, 'No embargo').
catalog_locator: p. 138, ch. 4 'Tone System of Ọ́lọ̀mà', §4.2.2.4.2 'High Tone in Ọ́lọ̀mà' (stress denial); p. 116, §4.1 (tone inventory)., re-extracted with p. 160 and p. 138.
catalog_quote: Initially, I had thought that syllable prominence plays an important role in tone assignment in Ọ́lọ̀mà, but Ọ́lọ̀mà is not a stress language. Nevertheless, the tonal assignment and tonal prominence scale presented by de Lacy (1999:5) states that a higher tone is more prominent than a lower tone ... It appears that word-final and utterance-final positions in Ọ́lọ̀mà are ‘weaker’ positions and will not attract the prominence of the high tone. I have abandoned this strategy because I cannot prove that certain syllables are weaker or stronger in the language, but it is worth experimenting to see whether metrical phonology could provide clarity. [p. 138] ... Ọ́lọ̀mà is a terraced level tone language with two contrastive tones, High or H marked by an acute sign [ ́] and Low or L marked by a grave sign [ ̀]. Ọ́lọ̀mà has two contrastive contour tones: falling tone [ ̂] and rising tone [ ̌]. Tone performs both lexical and grammatical functions in Ọ́lọ̀mà. [p. 116]
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: File is a 342-page text-layer PDF (Word-produced, dated 2023-03-23, author "japhet ajani"). Re-extracted p. 160 (printed p. 138) with extracted text: inside §4.2.2.4.2 "High Tone in Ọ́lọ̀mà" (heading confirmed in the TOC and body) the sentence reads exactly "Initially, I had thought that syllable prominence plays an important role in tone assignment in Ọ́lọ̀mà, but Ọ́lọ̀mà is not a stress language." The surrounding paragraph considers Franich 2021 / Liberman & Prince 1977 metrical prominence as an explanation for the ban on H in word-/utterance-final position, then says "I have abandoned this strategy because I cannot prove that certain syllables are weaker or stronger in the language", and…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Oloma has no word stress: the author states outright that it is not a stress language. Word prosody is tonal (terraced-level system, two contrastive level tones H and L plus falling and rising contours). The remark comes while considering, and rejecting, a metrical (prominence-based) account of why high tones are avoided word-finally; the author says he cannot show that any syllable is metrically stronger or weaker.
new_statements.exceptions: None. The author notes only that word-final and utterance-final positions appear 'weaker' in that they do not attract high tone, but explicitly abandons a metrical-prominence explanation.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level (tone assignment within words); the stress remark is a single explicit sentence inside a theoretical discussion of tonal asymmetry rather than a dedicated suprasegmentals subsection, but it is first-hand, from 11 months of fieldwork with 21 consultants and Praat-annotated data. No instrumental stress study.
new_statements.identity_note: Ajani 2023 describes Ọ́lọ̀mà as spoken in the Oloma community of Akoko-Edo (Edo State, Nigeria), near Ọ̀kpẹ̀ and Ghotuo; the dissertation argues Ọ́lọ̀mà and (Akoko-Edo) Ọ̀kpẹ̀ are distinct languages. This matches olom1241 directly; no dialect split is described.

tone_statements.citation: Akingbade, Olawale. 2025. Tone behavior of Oloma noun phrase. Paper presented at the Konstanz Linguistics Conference (KLC 2025), University of Konstanz, 9-10 October 2025. Abstract in: KLC2025 Book of Abstracts, pp. 12-13. (University of Michigan, Department of Linguistics; part of PhD research in progress on Oloma and Akuku.)
tone_statements.quote: This study investigates the tone behavior of noun phrases in Oloma [ɔ́lɔ̀mà], a Northwestern Edoid language. ... The results show that Oloma noun phrases exhibit a phrasal HL (High-Low) tonal melody, resulting in obligatory spreading of H and consistent lowering of the final tone within noun phrases (1a-c). ... When the final tone of a noun phrase is high, it undergoes downstep. ... I propose that the presence of a phrasal HL melody governing tone alternations in Oloma noun phrases constitutes phonological evidence for intonational structure in this two-tone language.
tone_statements.locator: KLC2025 Book of Abstracts (abstract 'Tone Behavior of Oloma Noun Phrase', paragraphs 1, 3 and 4)
tone_statements.summary: Two tones (H, L) — 'this two-tone language'; at NP level a phrasal HL melody: H spreads obligatorily and the NP-final tone is lowered; an NP-final H surfaces downstepped; noun + cardinal numeral or quantifier does not take the HL melody, but complex NPs with multiple modifiers do; lexical tones established in isolation (e.g. /HL/, /HLL/, /HHHHL/ nouns/adjectives). No statement about stress.
